title: Weighted timing offsets gave no clear mean lag prediction gain in 22 larval zebrafish
abstract: We tested whether regional timing offsets, weighted by each pair's correlation-curve slope, predict calcium lag patterns better than additive region timing values. We used 57 common regions in 22 public larval zebrafish recordings. Each model was fitted in one spontaneous segment and tested in another, in both directions. The mean weighted-minus-additive prediction score was 0.0033 (-0.0324 to 0.0303); exact two-sided p=0.8886; positive in 13/22 fish. Nine fish absent from the earlier lag study gave 0.0215 (-0.0019 to 0.0421). A model that combined both feature sets gave a mean score change of 0.0349 (0.0135 to 0.0555). The unrestricted weighted coefficient range was 2.04 to 5.74 volumes across fish. A timing-only covariance control left 80.5 percent of lag energy after additive adjustment, while the weighted model explained over 99.99 percent. Thus, an additive lag residual alone does not identify pair-specific neural transmission. This control does not establish the source of fish lags. Short recordings, slow calcium signals, large fitted coefficients, one experiment and a cross-animal projectome limit the result. Original code, aggregate evidence, figures, exact source hashes and separate external-data retrieval steps support reproduction.

Prior weighted lag projections address sampling precision. Our weights enter a model of fixed-lag correlation asymmetry, not a precision-weighted mean of peak-delay estimates.
